target: AG1’s claim that AI is good for society because it improves convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and workplace safety.
objection: AI’s benefits come with serious societal tradeoffs: automation can displace workers and weaken wages, AI can undermine critical thinking by encouraging people to outsource reasoning, it can entrench racial bias by amplifying historical inequities, and it creates dangerous privacy and surveillance risks; these harms outweigh the conveniences.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms jobs, critical thinking, bias outcomes, and privacy in ways that make it bad overall.
objection: Those harms are not inevitable; with proper design and governance, AI can reduce job displacement pressure through reskilling and new uses, strengthen learning when used as a tutor rather than an answer generator, reduce bias through auditing and fairness checks, and protect privacy through data minimization and access controls.

target: AG1’s claim that safeguards can make AI safe enough that it is good for society.
objection: The same problems are structurally likely to persist because incentives favor speed, scale, and data collection over safety and fairness; companies will underinvest in auditing and privacy, AI tutoring can still weaken critical thinking, bias can emerge after deployment, and privacy-preserving design is not the default.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms are structurally likely to persist and thus outweigh benefits.
objection: Society can change incentives through regulation and procurement so safeguards are enforceable: mandatory auditing, privacy-by-design requirements, and AI tutoring that requires student effort can make AI safer in practice and allow its benefits in health, accessibility, and safety to be realized.

target: AG1’s claim that mandated safeguards and governance can realistically make AI good overall.
objection: Regulation cannot outrun rapid deployment, enforcement is uneven, fairness and privacy are moving targets, responsibility is diffused across vendors and deployers, and the high-stakes harms are serious enough that possible fixes should not be treated as proof of net benefit.

target: AG2’s claim that imperfect enforcement means AI should be judged bad overall.
objection: AI need not be deployed all-or-nothing; society can use capability-limited, risk-managed deployment, including staged rollouts, human-in-the-loop oversight with real procedural authority, and tighter accountability, so benefits can be captured while harmful uses are restricted.

target: AG1’s claim that risk-managed, capability-limited deployment can keep AI harms contained.
objection: In practice, spillover is hard to prevent because AI models and infrastructure migrate into higher-stakes uses, human oversight becomes token under time pressure, staged pilots still harm real people and can entrench bias, and the biggest gains go to firms while costs fall on workers and minorities.

target: AG2’s claim that spillover and weak oversight make AI’s harms unavoidable.
objection: Governments and large buyers can impose use-case gating, substantive human oversight, and worker protections such as reskilling and wage support; liability and procurement rules can make expansion and harmful deployment harder, so spillover is not inevitable.

target: AG1’s claim that gating, oversight, liability, and worker protections can materially reduce AI’s harms.
objection: General-purpose AI systems are hard to compartmentalize, gating can be bypassed because the same model stack gets reused across contexts, human oversight is unreliable against persuasive outputs, worker protections are politically fragile, and privacy and bias risks remain systemic across the ecosystem.

target: AG2’s claim that systemic spillover makes AI net harmful.
objection: Stronger liability for deployers, purpose-limited sandboxed deployment, and AI used to monitor itself can reduce speed-to-market pressure and improve oversight; since AI has real upside for accessibility, health support, productivity, and safety, those controls support a good societal outcome.

target: AG1’s claim that liability, sandboxing, and AI-based auditing are enough to manage AI risks.
objection: Liability can be diluted through contracts and vendor chains, sandboxing fails because models and outputs are portable and reusable, AI auditing inherits the same biased data and assumptions that caused the harm, and widespread use of persuasive answer systems still erodes critical thinking at a cultural level.

target: AG2’s claim that AI should be opposed because of its harms.
objection: Holding back on AI also has costs: it withholds accessibility, health, and workplace-safety benefits from people who need them, and AI can also improve decision quality and fight misinformation through retrieval, citations, cross-checking, and structured feedback rather than just enabling answer machines.

target: AG1’s claim that the harms of AI do not outweigh its benefits, and that AI verification features offset critical-thinking concerns.
objection: Many benefits could be delivered by narrower, privacy-preserving technologies instead of general-purpose AI, and verification features often still lead to overreliance, misleading citations, and diminished skepticism; the remaining bias, privacy, and economic harms still dominate.

target: AG2’s claim that verification features and AI tutoring inevitably harm critical thinking.
objection: Source-grounded systems with retrieval and provenance, educational designs that require student effort, and systems that generate counterpoints and uncertainty prompts can prevent hallucination and dependence while improving understanding and information quality.

target: AG1’s claim that source-grounded systems and better instructional design make AI good overall.
objection: Citations and retrieval can reproduce biased or incomplete source material, students can game tutoring systems and learn to seek plausible outputs rather than understanding, many everyday benefits can be achieved with narrower software, and general AI concentrates power while exposing workers and communities to surveillance and biased outcomes.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is net bad overall because its risks likely outweigh its benefits.
objection: That conclusion relies on uncertain assumptions about implementation and enforcement, while the benefits of accessibility tools, health support, and safety improvements are concrete and immediate; on-device and privacy-preserving inference can also reduce the centralized data pipelines that drive surveillance risk.

target: AG1’s claim that on-device, privacy-preserving AI plus a burden-of-proof framing make AI good for society.
objection: On-device inference still depends on centralized model distribution, updates, telemetry, and analytics; privacy fixes do not address job pressure, outsourced reasoning, or biased outcomes; and model monoculture creates systemic risks that can spread harms widely and quickly.

target: AG2’s claim that AI should be judged by its harms because governance is imperfect.
objection: Human decisions are already imperfect and often less auditable than AI; AI can be logged and tested for error rates and group disparities, and standardized decision support can reduce inconsistency and some bias relative to current human-led systems.

target: AG1’s claim that AI is more auditable and consistent than human decision-making, so it may be good overall.
objection: Meaningful auditing is often impossible because vendors withhold training data assumptions and logs, decision support creates automation bias that changes human behavior, and at scale AI can amplify errors and inequities faster and farther than human decision-making.
